utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. May we hear in what case we take a deposition today, continuing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian and Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any obstacles to proceed with the deposition taking?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No obstacles on our side, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy. May I ask, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence to start.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would it be okay if I ask the Court if the ELMO may be lowered, please, or directing the... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, proceeding with some of our discussions yesterday, I'd like to clarify if I may some points in connection with both your testimony here in this matter and in prior cases. Initially, though, I'd like to ask you with respect to your book and articles and your reporting that you conducted subsequent to August 5th, 1992, although you did receive some fame and acclaim, if you will, for those reports, you also received some criticism, outspoken criticism, about the coverage and the effect, if you will, of your reporting. Do you know that or acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, objection, relevance whether someone criticised him outside the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I also can't see any relevance whether or not an author is criticised, which seems to be normal in this world.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may just have some latitude on this, Your Honour, I think the criticism goes to actually some foundational facts that the author purports he has observed and has recorded subsequent to that. Others, quite frankly, and we hope to present that within our case, respectfully, to Mr. Vulliamy, have specifically outlined certain criticisms of his opinions and as well as his impressions during his visit to Trnopolje and Omarska in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may I ask to try the Defence takes press this criticism on the basis of facts relevant for the decision in our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Some of the criticism, if I may, respectfully, Mr. Vulliamy, and I recognise that people do have differences of opinion from time to time, have identified your reporting and your book as being one-sided, unobjective, distorted, contrived, and misleading. You're familiar with those. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those words in particular are yours. There have been criticisms, again, your word, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Are you familiar with Thomas Deichmann the German journalist who has reviewed ad nauseum, I would say both the videos and your work. Was he complimentary or critical of your work?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, those were two questions. I would ask counsel to ask the witness one question and allow him to answer the first question before the second question is asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed in this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to answer your first question, I am familiar with Thomas Deichmann. I have not met him. I totally agree with your word "ad nauseum." And what I think you said critical, most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify a point. It's not my word critical. I wanted to distinguish whether it was a criticism or a complimentary review he did of your work both the reporting and articles of August 7th, 1992, and subsequently your book "Seasons in Hell" of 1994. Also, are you familiar with Oliver Hotensia [phoen] who wrote extensively --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to stop these line of questions. As already indicated and based on the objection by the OTP, this is not relevant to our case. We are not to make recommendations on books or disqualification on books. We have to discuss the facts in our case. Please, restrict your questions to this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The criticisms, if you will, that were attributed to your writings and works and reporting and/or coverage of your visits to Trnopolje involve the issue of a barbed-wire fence, did it not?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there has been --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Objection, Mr. Vulliamy, if I could just remind you again to pause not just for the interpreter but to allow me at times to make an objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour just ruled that the questions of criticisms by outsiders is not the subject of testimony today. We have not put into evidence the numerous very distinguished individuals that have given acclaim to Mr. Vulliamy. That's not relevant to the case. Your Honours decide on the credibility of the witness. And the last question began immediately after your objection about the criticism. So my objection is that counsel is disregarding your order.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, if I may, Your Honour, I understood your order that if we are going to highlight any of the criticisms or any of the opinions by other distinguished members of the press both international and in Europe, specifically in Yugoslavia, that we should be specific about it. Certainly, it wasn't an intent on our part to ignore or to overlook the Court's ruling. Our issue then became specific, and I was going to highlight one of many issues which were specific factually, which we believe may have some relevance since those issues appear within the indictment to ask this witness. We would be happy to move along. We have three other areas to cover. However, I don't want to be precluded later from presenting evidence on this since from time to time, the OTP has requested that we put our case before the witness so that he could come out and explain to us why this is this differing of opinion and why -- and how is it possible that there would be a diametrically opposed opinion on something that should be rather straightforward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we shouldn't confuse two aspects. No doubt, it's the right for the Defence when presenting their case to present other views and other authors on this same issue. But it's not to discuss on the basis of other books and commentaries on the books -- on the book we have in part before us the witness. And it is necessary that you restrict yourself to the issues we had and the facts we have heard during the examination-in-chief. And if you want, for example, you started with barbed-wire fence, indeed, it's not interesting at all now in the presence of this witness if everybody criticised on this point. Please, if you feel that there is a problem, ask on this fence, and on that what the witness has seen there and what the witness has experienced there and what the witness has heard there. But not by introducing this through the criticism, the alleged criticism, of third persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, during your visit on August 5th, 1992, did you at any time interview any of the detainees or witnesses at Trnopolje camp in order to determine when the so-called barbed-wire fence was erected?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. The so-called barbed-wire fence was a barbed-wire fence or a fence reinforced by barbed wire, but I observed that there two, if you like, generations of barbed wire, the one fairly old and another reinforced and new.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, during the interview and taping of the detainees at Trnopolje camp that certain individuals, and we will play the tape in a moment, were leaning upon the fence with their hands on the actual wire? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any particular scene of people leaning on the fence, but I wouldn't be surprised if they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A barbed-wire fence is supposedly placed there to prohibit people from leaving. It has markings on the exact wire which would cause some harm to an individual who tried to either climb over the fence or get through the fence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. However, I now know, and I did not observe then, but I now know that the fencing confining these prisoners was not reinforced by barbed wire all the way around the compound. I think you're aware, sir, but I will answer your questions, that this has been the case -- the subject of litigation in my country and has been settled -- those who -- well, those who repeated -- you mentioned Mr. Deichmann, who repeated his points were defeated in court for libel. To answer you question, I accept that a barbed-wire fence is not pleasant to lean on. If they were leaning on a fence, as you say they were, perhaps it was not the bit of the fence that had the barbed wire on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Clarify for me what portions, and I know you testified about this under oath on in a prior trial, isn't it true that it was on one side that this barbed-wire fence has been erected?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, it was on at least one side, or one and possibly two. I now that it was not all the way around the area, the fenced-off area or compound in which those men were quite clearly confined.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can ask the technical booth to run the tape that we previously set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, do you know the number of the tape we are going to play?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe it's S -- if the Court registrar would be kind enough...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's S157.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This, Mr. Vulliamy, I think as you testified in your direct is the queue that you observed in front of the police station that you testified to. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell from this picture which --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we stop right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know what the purpose of videotaping this woman who has a candle lit in front of her was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not, as I think I said, running the ITN -- making any decision about what ITN did or didn't film.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you make any observations subsequent to your visit to Prijedor on August 5th, 1992, to determine who this woman in particular was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you make or at any time learn that this is a woman of Serbian descent who placed a candle on the road because her son had been killed there by the name of Mrs. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I had not heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we please continue to run the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fast forward a little, please. Stop there, please. Sorry, can we back up to the start of that meeting. Stop right there. And then forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, at this point, there's an introduction made of Dr. Stakic as being president of the Municipal Assembly. My question to you, having been present there, at any time during this meeting, sir, was there any indication or identification of anyone being a member of a "Crisis Committee"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we covered this yesterday. There was a mention of crisis -- I recall -- committee. I stand to be corrected staff. But no one in -- no individual. It was used on the way -- as I recall, to the best of my recollection, on the way up, but not in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's my question. Specifically in the room, at any time, do your notes or your memory reflect that there was any discussion about this "crisis committee"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection in the room, no. And from what I've gathered from the notes, that at least the photocopied pages that we had yesterday or whenever it was, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, your numerous articles that you wrote identifying the individuals in Prijedor indicate from time to time that Dr. Stakic was a mayor. Do you know and did you subsequently learn that there is no such position in the municipality of Prijedor in 1992, or even today, of a title "mayor"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the word was used in the translations that I have recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, from your recollection, and being there at the time of the events in which you're testifying to, were you ever introduced to Dr. Stakic as being a mayor of the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I recall -- I have noted president of, I think, the committee, and I do recall the word "mayor," and of course he used it or at least was translated of having used it at our later meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And that would be the meeting of February 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's that same meeting where you start by writing in your aide-memoires that Colonel Arsic told you specifically that Dr. Stakic was the person in charge of Omarska camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've already been over this, and I stand by my account that he was introduced to us as the senior official in the body whose authority we would need to get into the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can continue to play the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fast forward this portion. Stop, please. Back up a little bit. Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now you mentioned yesterday, and I want to know if it's depicted on this tape that Dr. Kovacevic at one point exerting his influence at the meeting and over individuals at the meeting simply instructed Dr. Stakic to shut up so he could proceed at which point Dr. Stakic conceded, and Dr. Kovacevic proceeded to talk. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or as you put it, when you were defending Dr. Kovacevic, he wanted to make sure he continued in order to finish what he was saying, yes, he did shut him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, Mr. Vulliamy: You didn't agree with me four years ago. Are you agreeing with me now that the gesture by Dr. Kovacevic was simply a gesture of politeness or was it certainly a gesture of control? Because I vividly remember debating with you that very issue, and you disagreeing and insisting upon the fact that Dr. Kovacevic was the man in control, and here is a vivid example of how he controlled not only the meeting but all the individuals around him.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Which side or which story would you like this Court now to believe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence, as we do it usually, to quote correctly your question at that time and the answer at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's quite lengthy, Your Honour, but we have it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know, I can read myself. But it's interesting, and we should really go into details if the Defence wants to enter this terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm limited in my time, Your Honour. I'd like to move on to other points. If the Court looks at the record, it is Mr. Vulliamy who offered this as some sort of conciliatory effort on his part to say that there was an exchange. It's certainly not in issue since we have his testimony that Dr. Kovacevic on numerous occasions that he has written and testified was the person in control, that Dr. Kovacevic on numerous occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You shouldn't put forward arguments. Please give us -- indicate -- I'm quite sure you have the page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The cross begins on page 903, Your Honour. Goes on actually for approximately a day and a half. I can try to highlight for the Court the area. We could come back to it as my colleague Mr. Cirkovic will assist us in finding if the Court doesn't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, let me ask you also, during the Kovacevic trial, you were asked specifically on page 819, for the Court, whether you left Prijedor immediately after your visit to Trnopolje camp, and you said, yes, and that you went back to Belgrade. And then you were asked specifically: "Did you ever return to Prijedor?" And your answer was: "Yes, several years later, in 1996." Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- in terms of staying in Prijedor to hold meetings, yes, indeed. But I think I've already testified and will -- apologies for repeating myself, on the way to picking up the convoy of deportees went through Prijedor in what would have been -- well, later on that month, August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So your testimony when you testified in Kovacevic, it was a question that you didn't understand, and you simply said I returned to Prijedor in 1996 when, in fact, you had returned to Prijedor less than three weeks after your visit to the Trnopolje camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered the question with reference to when I went to Prijedor to work in Prijedor, to conduct -- to be -- to stay in Prijedor for a duration of time. When I went through Prijedor and I did go through Prijedor in August 1992, it was not to Prijedor; it was through Prijedor. But yes, I was physically in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, if I may: Your discussion on August 5th with Colonel Arsic and Major Milutinovic involving the Manjaca camp, do you know where Manjaca camp was located?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Prijedor area. I don't know exactly. It had been already located in newspaper articles, but I don't know exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: My question is do you know in which municipality it was in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know which municipality it's in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me turn, if I may, briefly with the limited time that we have to the February 1996 meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- That you had with Dr. Stakic, among others? Did Roger Cohen of the New York Times also keep and maintain his own records of the notes relating to the meeting between Dr. Stakic, yourself, and Mr. Cohen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer for whether he kept or retained them. But he was taking notes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But did you take the original papers from him subsequent to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take any notes physically from him, no, but we compared our notes afterwards, yes. I didn't take them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he still has possession of those notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, during your meeting with Dr. Stakic in February 1996, both from your contemporaneous notes and your aide-memoires, did you at any time discuss this concept of "Crisis Committee" with him? And if so, please point it out in the record.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you like to have both your contemporaneous notes and your aide-memoires to assist you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be a good idea if the Court-- if I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please provide the witness with I would think DP-5, DP-6, and DPD, I think it was 2, the aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DPD-4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I think you'd like me to have the shorthand notes of the meeting with Mr. Stakic in February 1996. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Both your aide-memoires as well as the contemporaneous notes that you took.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, sir, if you could hold on a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That'd be the last five pages of that document.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forgive me, sir. It's not actually here. I may need to... It Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. looks like that, and it has got "Stakic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be DP-6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Your Honours. Sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Vulliamy, there's a question pending. If you'd like, I can restate it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you kindly. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course. At any time within your contemporaneous notes or your aide-memoires, do you indicate a discussion with Dr. Stakic about this concept of "Crisis Committee"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's in the notes or not. Do you want me to look through?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to, if you don't mind. You read them into the record yesterday. Do you have a recollection of certain events that occurred in February of 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall reading them into the record. And to the best of my recollection, I didn't talk about a Crisis Committee or Staff from these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time during your meeting with Dr. Stakic in February of 1996, did you discuss with him the role of the police and military vis-a-vis the detention centres?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was that a decision that was predetermined on your part, or just an area that you were not interested in?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither. It didn't come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time during your meeting with Dr. Stakic discuss with him the police chief who you met who you wished to interview during this same time period by the name of Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time with Dr. Stakic ask for clarification as to who may have been in control of Omarska or Trnopolje in light of, sir, your articles, namely, the August 7th, 1992, article which is in the record wherein you identify Dr. Kovacevic as the person being in control and having authority to have people gain access to the certain camps, and then your subsequent book in 1994? Did you ever ask Dr. Kovacevic to clarify that issue for you, if there was any doubt about whether it was Dr. Kovacevic or Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was introduced to them as I think I've said as president and vice-president of the same body and was, I think, -- and fairly inferred that here was a chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll discuss your inferences in light of the background that you shared with us yesterday at the commencement of your cross-examination. However, did you ever at any time discuss with Dr. Stakic the military role of either Colonel Arsic or Major Milutinovic in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any conversation with Dr. Stakic about either Major Milutinovic or Colonel Arsic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Since you were in Bosnia in 1992 or in Prijedor, and in February 1996, did you, sir, as an objective foreign correspondent investigate at any time the Serbian refugees that were being displaced or deported from Central Bosnia and Croatia during that time period?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, indeed. I was one of the first journalists -- well, actually, driving through the eastern part of what was then being called Croatian-controlled Croatia, and the Krajina area which was under the Croatian/Serbian control, and wrote one of the first articles observing a significant military buildup, menacing military buildup by Croatian forces in the Gospic area that seemed to suggest an impending offensive. And wrote another article I might add extremely critical of the Croatian forces soon after they got into the town of Knin setting large amounts of Serbian refugees on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time, sir, write an article or investigate whether there were any Muslim camps which were holding Serbian citizens?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to all of you to repeat myself. I did go in search of one that was mentioned by Professor Koljevic in Belgrade. I haven't seen any documents since yesterday to give further details. But to the best of my recollection, the place was called Tarcin. What I do remember is the place was a tunnel in which people were supposedly being kept, and I couldn't find any. That is not to say that I am saying now that there were not such camps because I have since heard of the Celebici camp which you mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of any camps in existence in 1992 since you were actually in Sarajevo in August of 1992 that existed in Sarajevo which held Serbian citizens?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Sarajevo itself. I don't recall being told about them. The ones that Professor Koljevic talked about were over on what I would call the other side, further away from the capital. And forgive me for repeating myself, but the one that he was most concerned about and emphasised was the camp near Caplinja which I did visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time since you mentioned issues of hierarchy and chain of command study or establish what the actual chain of command was in Prijedor in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said chain of command, I was referring to the terms president and vice-president or, as I will stand by, alternatively mayor and deputy mayor seemed to mean much the same. And as in any political authority, you have a president and a deputy. You have the man at the top and the number two. And my country, there's a prime minister and a deputy prime minister and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's take your country, if you will. In a city or a small town within Britain, would there be any influence of a local politician, whether he be the president or deputy or mayor, to have any influence over a regional command structure such as a military colonel or major?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is not relevant. Not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time, sir, during your investigation giving us your opinion as to the hierarchy or chain of command did you ever study what the military chain of command was in Prijedor in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know any military by ranks. I did not -- Colonel Arsic was introduced as the senior military presence in that area. If there was a general in Prijedor above him, then my instincts would say that the colonel was not in charge. But that's the military authorities. Again, I repeat myself, my apologies. Dr. Stakic and Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Drljaca were introduced to us as and later by Colonel Arsic as the civilian authorities in charge of the nonmilitary operations in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time study or review or investigate the police hierarchy or structure in Prijedor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say study, investigate, and review, it would have been certainly to my advantage to have been allowed to stay in the area a little bit longer. But this was not possible. What I'm saying, once again, in answer to your question is that we were introduced by Colonel Arsic to the civilian authorities, those three gentlemen, as those on whose authority we would go to Omarska if we were going to be allowed to go. I apologise if I'm long-winded. But the short answer to your question is I was not given the chance to study, investigate, or review the command structure. I think some of the television pictures we saw in Omarska the other day gave us a pretty good idea of what the atmosphere was, and that's certainly what I recall. We were persona non grata in the town. So, in-depth investigation was neither logistically possible nor, I would imagine, possible anyway, nor welcome on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You shared with us subsequent to August 1992 you have become more knowledgeable in the events of both the Prijedor municipality and the detention centres at Omarska and Trnopolje, and I know that you testified in the Tadic case about various issues that we covered. My question to you is not limited to that one day and those three hours that you may have spent in both the camps, did you subsequent to that, sir, do any analysis to determine what the hierarchy, structure, was between the police, namely, the MUP in the Prijedor municipality with the political establishment that you've identified? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a long question, and I can't answer it with one word. I did become more knowledgeable of the events in the Prijedor municipality. I was not able to go, as I think I've already said, I was refused access to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as it was then called. So I was not able to study, as you put, the specifics of the command structure. However, I was able to become more knowledgeable of what was going on in the Prijedor municipality on the basis of meeting very large numbers of survivors of the camps at Omarska and Trnopolje, bereaved relatives of those who had perished in those camps, and other information I could glean from the tens of thousands of people coming over the road I myself had gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the record, we've basically found the portion where there was a discussion on the gesture of Mr. Vulliamy and that appears on pages 1128. I am told that it proceeds for approximately 25 to 30 pages. I'm not sure if the Court would like me to read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we first, please, we have bundles of papers here before us. What date was it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: July 17th, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Unfortunately the bundle I have in my hand concludes the 15th of July. And then let me see the next bundle. Bundle by bundle. Could you please repeat the page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 1128, Your Honour. 1-1-2-8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask exactly, what about this gesture that seems to be public domain in this premises a discussion on this gesture?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think perhaps if we put the question to the witness, but I'd be happy to give the Court a summary of what I recall and have reviewed in connection with this gesture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would prefer to have it before me black and white and not a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We've highlighted the cross-examination questions in connection with the gesture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For example, on page 1131, a gesture and how it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The following page, Your Honour, if I may, 1132, there is a discussion by Mr. Vulliamy recollecting the gesture, and this is a follow-up on questions put to him during questioning by Michael Keegan on direct examination wherein he stated and confirmed, I believe, both yesterday and today that he thought the gesture was to shut up Dr. Stakic, and he uses those very words. And that appears on page 781 of the direct examination transcript which I believe we covered yesterday during our initial cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Please proceed on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you at any time during your testimony both in Kovacevic and here today and yesterday have any doubt that Dr. Kovacevic was commanding and controlling the entire meeting and by virtue of his gesture by raising his hand was indicating for Dr. Stakic to shut up?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was raising his hand to get Dr. Stakic to shut up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Dr. Stakic, although from time to time you've identified him in some of your articles as being Dr. Kovacevic's boss, Dr. Stakic certainly responded by doing what?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stopped talking, even though he was Dr. Kovacevic's boss. He was a man of fewer words than Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, based upon your ruling, or our understanding of it, and retaining our right to have the complete video played during the Defence case and calling the witnesses such as those that we've identified Thomas Deichmann, Joan Phillips, Christopher Bennett, and Mike Hume, we have no further questions for this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask the Prosecution, additional questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, briefly, Your Honour. The video that was just played by the Defence this morning, if we could back that up from the point it stopped a bit, I'd like to play what I believe is the gesture that was just referred to. Is it possible also to hand out the transcript - I don't know if the Court has it - the transcript of that tape, 1402. One of our deposition exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If it was video S157, so it should be -1, not deposition exhibit. It was an original exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this be backed up, and I'll tell the booth when to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask that we, in order to avoid double discussing this issue here, stop only when the witness enters the room and is welcomed. A little bit further back, please. So then start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could we stop the videotape. Mr. Vulliamy, if you put on your headphones to channel 4, you could hear the video, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, did you just see the gesture by Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is that the gesture that you were speaking of in your testimony in the Kovacevic trial?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just one other question: Do you recall early in that videotape, someone standing up and pointing in the direction of where you and the our journalists were?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to play video S187. But just while that's getting ready, questions for you, just to introduce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You were asked several times about various titles that were used, president and mayor, by the Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we can now play S187, there's just a minute or two of that I'd like to play. I don't know if Your Honours -- I don't think the transcript is necessary, but there is a transcript to this also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sorry, stop the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt -- (a), if we're going to have the tape played and we're going to rely on the interpreter who was there to interpret for us, that's one thing. But even in the prior tape, there were things that Dr. Kovacevic said which I think are important which the Defence are going to bring up in our Defence case that are not translated such as the fact, as I'm sure the OTP knows from prior matters, that Dr. Kovacevic says: "Despite the fact that you were given the authority to come here and there's nothing we can do about that," et cetera, whatever the implications may be of that, similarly here, when Dr. Stakic clearly states he's the president of the Municipal Assembly, that should be interpreted for the Court if it's in relation to the questions that are being asked of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I agree a hundred per cent. I was indicating that I forgot there was no translation on this tape. May the translation be handed out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So we can begin at the beginning of the transcript, if the tape could be backed up and we'll play it from the beginning again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: First Mr. Vulliamy, are you familiar with a journalist who, I believe, worked in Bosnia and was one of the reporters for the programme "Dispatches"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the gentleman is by the name of Harriman [phoen] but I know him actually from when I was in television, not from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If everyone is ready and has a transcript. Is the Defence ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all the tape I wanted to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, were Dr. Stakic's words on that video consistent with the information you received in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The Defence also asked you about information you learned about Prijedor from other sources after August the 5th of 1992. And you told us about your trip to Travnik. While in Travnik, did you see or hear of other convoys of refugees from the municipality of Prijedor arriving in that town?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were coming in continuously. When I was working in and returning to Travnik in 1992, into 1993 period, and indeed, trickles of deportees were still coming over into Travnik, over the mountain into Travnik when I returned yet again as late as 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You indicated that you arrived in Travnik on the 17th of August. Do you recall approximately how long you stayed in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one night because we needed to get to a telephone and to do that, you had to drive all the way to the coast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At some time, were you in Travnik in 1992, and did you hear of any stories of a convoy on a -- a few days after, approximately the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Travnik sometime -- pardon me, the late 20s of August, if not the first week of September. I don't know the exact date. And had heard and asked about the convoys and heard that on one night, some - and the figures being quoted at the time were about 200 - people had been murdered, massacred, on an exact same convoy as ours on the mountain which by then I knew was Mount Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just one very small detail, but I think it's important to come back to this. May the usher please present exhibits S2 and S3 to the witness, and may the map surrounded by pictures be put on the ELMO, first, this part. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we actually found a much larger map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have prepared this specially because the early days of this case, we had headlines indicating what the building is. So we took the liberty to redact this. Yes. If you could focus on the two photos on the upper left-hand side, please, the photos, please. Yes, closer, closer, if you could zoom this. Yes, that's fine. Are you able, on the basis of these photos, of these stills, to identify any of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll do my very best. And Your Honours, they look like many other buildings of their kind in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe it's better if you look at the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, could I. I can't say that I actually recognise the building but because of where we are, if it's one of the buildings in the square complex around Prijedor, then so be it. But I don't recall that view of that particular building. I was never at any distance from the building that I suspect it is, but I'm not going to say that I recognise that exact building particularly. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you for being so clear. And if you can't identify it, you can't. So may we then, please, play Exhibit DP-4, the videotape. It should be queued at a special point. In order not to lose time, let's turn first to another issue, and may Madam Registrar please tell me if the video is ready, when the video will be ready. One other additional question, please, totally different issue: You mentioned that you were accompanied on your tour first to Omarska and then to Trnopolje by the same persons in that convoy. But we did not yet Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discuss whom did you meet in Trnopolje? Did you meet there, as you did in Omarska, persons you would, after your own assessment, regard as the responsible persons for Trnopolje, to the best of your own recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no -- to the best of my recollection, there was no individual such as that as I remember very clearly as Mr. Meakic in Omarska. There were quite clearly more senior or more junior guards around the area in a variety of uniforms. But their seniority could only be, as it were, inferred by their deportment rather than any official introductions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The video is ready? No, it's not. Then a more general question: We saw numerous videos, and one issue in this entire case and in other cases is that it is alleged that numerous evidence may have been forged, documents may have been forged, and there were also rumours that videos in the past had been forged in order to support the one or the other side. Amongst those videos you saw today, especially - and yesterday and the day before - can you state that these videos reflect the reality, or did you have the impression that there was some forgery, or were there ever indications or allegations that these videos were forged?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address you on this. I have been more than aware of, indeed, I have been -- I'm trying to find the right words for the courtroom that are presentable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Don't hesitate.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've become all too familiar with the allegations that you're talking about. They began with someone whose name has already been mentioned, but I don't think it's appropriate for me to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, don't hesitate.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Well, they appeared first in a German magazine authored by - and it's not me that's bringing up the name, it was the Defence - a Mr. Deichmann. They accused principally ITN, but also myself, of forgery, fabrication of all kinds. And there was -- well, not just criticism as the Defence said, but quite a hullabaloo of what came to be, as at least I saw it from my position, likewise ITN, a highly didactic and highly motivated attempt to dilute, and to use a fairly highly charged word - but I'm going to use it - to deny the severity of what was going on in those camps and of what we did and what we more importantly did not see in those camps which has been -- well, testified to me but not in the legal sense. ITN chose to take legal action against the publication of these allegations which were surrounded by all forms of public meetings and picketing of my office and those of ITN. And there was a legal action for libel over precisely this matter that Your Honour raises of forgery and injudicious editing, and the case was settled unanimously by jury in the High Court in London, in ITN's favour and against the publication which had repeated the allegations of forgery and so on by -- well, ITN specifically, but I was also implicated by a magazine by the name of "Living Marxism". ITN won. They lost. But I fear the allegations continue on the internet and elsewhere, and well, I find them repellant in -- well, I find them deeply offensive. If I may add an opinion, and it is an opinion in answer to your question, deeply offensive to myself and ITN, but much more importantly to what was actually going on in those camps. And it is quite frankly a language which cuts a raw nerve. And yes, to answer your question, more briefly, I am more than aware of those allegations. And I refute them utterly. ITN refutes them utterly because I can speak for them because that's their footage you're asking about. The footage is a fair representation of what was going on in Omarska. Actually, if any, it was an unfairly positive, as I now know, rendering of what was going on in the camp. And more important, I think in answer to Your Honours and a Bench of Judges, the matter also has been settled by the High Court in London.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But let's concentrate on those clips we saw during, as mentioned yesterday, the day before, and today, anything you saw on the video which is not covered by your recollection.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were other film crews there from Bosnian Serb television. I'm aware of other footage. I am aware that the purpose of other footage is to try and give some idea that the men in that part of the Trnopolje camp, that particular compound, were the - shall we say - the rather -- the men in worse condition were being kept were in some way free to come and go, or were not confined. It is certainly -- well, you know, established that they were confined, at least in this case I mentioned before. Is there other footage? Yes. Does the other footage that there is a fence there that is not covered by barbed wire? Yes. I now know that. At the time I was talking to people through a fence that did have barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, to concentrate on this issue, you saw numerous videos here in the courtroom, do they reflect that what you, in fact, saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon me for being verbose, yes apart from the videos of Omarska, and I now know those to be unrepresentatively positive. Trnopolje, yes. We saw fences with barbed wire and without barbed wire, and I think that the videos that have been presented today are representative of what I recall as being the conditions and situation in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us turn now to the video apparently ready for being played. May I ask to start the video. A little bit back, please. May it be winded back. Stop. Stop. And now proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Stop here, please. Can you on the basis of this - now it's a still even - identify the building?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- in my answer, respectfully, Your Honour, I now heard it labelled as Banja Luka on the film. To the best of my recollection, this is Prijedor, and certainly there was a long line of women in Prijedor. I'm going to answer your question by saying there was a long line of women in Prijedor. I remember it. I interviewed them. As with the still picture you showed me, I can't identify the actual building. If I wasn't in this courtroom and someone showed me a picture of that building, I would not say: "Oh, yes, that's a building in Prijedor." I'm afraid I can't say I recognise the building. If there are two long lines of women, one in Banja Luka and one in Prijedor, then I can only answer your question, Your Honour, by saying there was a long line of women in Prijedor which I know because I remember it very well and interviewed them. And if there was another long line of women in Banja Luka, then, Your Honour, I can only say there were two long lines of women. I can't help more than that really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a fair answer. May I ask, is there any additional questions? No, then let me finally come to the point we discussed, especially this morning, even gestures and reaction to gestures. In common-law system, the role of the accused is normally not highlighted in the way and explored in a way compared to civil-law system. Therefore, it's the Judges' interest to get a deeper insight in the personality of an accused person. From your own assessment, as far as we heard you met Dr. Stakic twice and you have met numerous persons in other environments, you're a man of the word, how would you describe the personality of Dr. Stakic, especially opposed to others you met in the area and you met in Prijedor? Please, if possible, based on facts, based on facts during your meeting in 1992 and in 1996.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll only answer on the basis of fact because I can't claim to know Dr. Stakic. There was one meeting as you know with several people in the room. Sorry. And only one other meeting with fewer people. Nor do I feel I have the right to psychoanalyse. But to help you, Your Honour, with the group at the August 1992 meeting, he and Colonel Arsic were certainly those more in control of themselves, more restrained and in a way robust in their -- in their composure, whereas Mr. Drljaca and Mr. Kovacevic were far more demonstrative as we've seen, but that is also my recollection. As regards other figures in the Bosnian Serb power hierarchy, if you like, I thought that - and this is my impression, I add - that Dr. Stakic was, yes, in control of his feelings and of his words, in a way that was menacing in a way, but not as -- as -- as physically menacing as some other people I had the dubious fortune to meet. In 1996, after the -- a fairy remarkable conversation with Dr. Kovacevic, certainly my view that Dr. Stakic was a man more in control of himself and of certainly the situation in that room than Dr. Kovacevic had been in control of himself was confirmed, and both my colleague and myself found the atmosphere in that room during that 1996, February 1996 meeting, with Dr. Stakic and his friend who I was then later told was some sort of security or police officer, not a lawyer or a health official, to be much more menacing and threatening. However, I would add that in terms of the bellicosity, or the overt bellicosity of other people in the Bosnian Serb structure that I had the chance to meet, and I didn't meet many for reasons I've explained; I wasn't allowed on the territory, he was certainly less of that overtly aggressive or rhetorical nature. If that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If I may, you mentioned, and you noted it, and you read it out on the basis of your own notes, you mentioned the father and the grandfather of Dr. Stakic. Do you have the impression, based on this, and probably it comes to your mind when discussing the issue of father and grandfather, to what extent there was a basis for the development of Dr. Stakic in a certain direction on historic events, on what he experienced during his childhood?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I have to infer a little bit here, but I can also relate specifically to what was said in that conversation with Dr. Stakic and with that with Dr. Kovacevic and others. And I think it has been put on the record that I found this family history extremely interesting. And I think that for what it's worth, the experience of many Serbs in the Second World War inevitably has stung a generation to which Dr. Stakic and Dr. Kovacevic belongs. And I think Dr. Kovacevic -- sorry, this isn't to answer your question about Dr. Stakic, but in general, he said he spent some time as a child, whether he was born there or not, in a concentration camp, in a death camp. And Dr. Stakic also said that his father had been killed by the Croatian NDH Ustasha. And I think there's no doubt that this horrific experience that that generation suffered did create, you know, certainly a sensitivity or call it paranoia. And in the longer cycle of history in that area, yet another sort of turn of the gyre or the wheel because this toing and froing had been going on for some time throughout history. However, based on the many conversations I've had about what was happening in the Prijedor area, while conceding from the basis of my knowledge that there was -- there were some Muslim fighters in the area, and also based on the knowledge of what happened during the whole history of Yugoslavia and specifically Serbia and the Serbian -- I want to be clear, can I in parenthesis, I mean Serbian nationalists, I do not mean all Serbs. I think it's important to stress that for instance in Sarajevo, when the call came to join Karadzic, some 90.000 effectively at the beginning at least refused to do so, wanted nothing to do with this. So I'm talking about a specific policy. So when I say the Serbian side, I don't mean the Serbian people -- I'm convinced -- get to the point. I'm convinced there's a notion of being stung by that experience for this generation during the Second World War. Yes, there were a few Muslim fighters in the Prijedor area for sure. That they were taking up arms in resistance, something that had started off in Belgrade -- won't mention any names -- and had come across the Drina River into Eastern Bosnia with terrifying ferocity and was also breaking out in the Prijedor/Banja Luka region with I now know to be terrifying ferocity, whether there's a connection between that and the Second World War, perhaps as Dr. Kovacevic himself said, perhaps this is something for the psychiatrists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, as to the fact that sometimes by, as just putting an arrow in your notes, from this I understand that your notes didn't cover the entire conversation, to the best of your recollection, was there any discussion what brought Dr. Stakic to join the SDS, and was ever discussed the issue of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbian Radical Party, there was no conversation about any difference between those two parties to the best of my recollection. There is a note at the bottom of one of the pages I noticed about the Socialist Party. But I don't recall any particular conversation about the SDS or the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the parties, are there additional questions emanating from the line of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes the taking deposition of your testimony. And I have to thank you very much for, yes, it's now the fourth time you are here in the courtroom. But I think it's important for both parties, and I want especially to express my gratitude for this fair way of putting questions to this witness knowing very well that it's -- it might be a little bit difficult. You met before in another case, and you had once again to dispute now from another point of view the same areas. To conclude, it was really helpful, and it's for us to thank you very much. This concludes the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And we reconvene for the purpose of the next taking of a deposition at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It will take a minute before these blinds are open. I don't know whether has introduced to you who is who in this courtroom. You should know we have to your left-hand side Defence counsel and Dr. Stakic. We have to your right-hand side the Office of the Prosecutor, their counsel. Persons sitting behind are legal officers of the Chamber. In front of us, you have the usher, legal officer of the Chamber, and Madam Registrar. And today, we are sitting in this composition as to the fact that unfortunately one of our Judges, normally the Bench is composed of three Judges, one of our Judges is ill. He will only be back on Monday. So just that you know who the persons are here in the courtroom. May I ask you, what is your actual profession? Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a lawyer. Currently, I work at the council for construction of flats in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the entire testimony, when you say you are a lawyer, it goes without saying, and you may know yourself, that in case there might be a question you have the impression that the answer could be a self-incriminating one, then you are not obliged to answer this question. We have then to discuss whether or not your right to remain silent on certain questions only is applicable. But I don't believe that in your case, we will have any problems with this. You have heard already in or have read in the invitation letter what it's all about, what will be the line of questions. And therefore, let us please start to ask you to tell us in context what was your professional development, your family development until 1992? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to school in Prijedor where I completed my primary education and my secondary education. I went on to study law at the faculty of law in Sarajevo. Upon the completion of my studies, I worked with the municipal organs, municipal administrative organs. I mostly dealt with issues related to property and land ownership. Mostly urban real estate envisaged for the construction of business premises in the town. In the period between 1980 and 1990, I worked at the council for the construction of the town. In 1991 and 1992, I worked as a secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Since 1993, I have again worked at the council for the construction of the town. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In an ordinary setting of an ordinary criminal court, I would never dare to ask this question. But for the purposes of this case, it's relevant, and may I ask you, what is your ethnic and religious background?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a Serb by nationality, and I'm not a religious person. I'm an atheist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I understand from your answer that you are now still working for the construction of the town. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we immediately turn to that what you mentioned. You said in 1991, 1992, I worked as a secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Can you please tell us, once again, in your own words and in context how it came to this development. Who invited you to work there and you were assigned to certain persons, or you worked in general in the Municipal Assembly? What was the scope of your work as a secretary in this Municipal Assembly? Could you please tell us in a detailed way what, from your point of view, are the most important parts of your work and please start with the development bringing you in 1991 to this assembly.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990, a law was passed to abolish the town construction company. So I was forced to look for a different job. I received an offer from an acquaintance, or perhaps it's better to say he phoned me to tell me that the SDS who were entitled to the position -- to appoint a person to the position of the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, that is, they had the power to appoint a person qualified to hold such a post. No one ever talked to me on behalf of the party, absolutely not. I did not even attend the session itself, the session of the assembly, at which the appointments were made public, the appointment for the post of the secretary. A number of colleagues of mine asked me why I hadn't come, I hadn't attended the session. I said no one had invited me in the first place. Still, I did take up the offer. It was difficult to find a job in any of the other companies still around. My opinion was that the job of secretary was not a very attractive job for a lawyer because what the job was really about was hard work where the secretary runs a very complicated service with only a handful of people to assist him, and the job of those people was to technically prepare the sessions of the assembly. And what that meant was when a session was announced, the agenda would be prepared as well as the items that would be discussed during the session. A technical service made copies of all these things using the technology at its disposal, put all these things in envelopes, and delivered the envelopes with the materials to the deputies. So the technical part of the service's activity was run, managed, by the secretary. And the job was to record the work of the assembly. And thereafter, to organise for a transcript of the session's work by a typist and to make copies of the decisions adopted at meetings, at sessions, to put a stamp on them, and then further these decisions to the municipal bodies which were then to process these decisions or conclusions. In practical terms, there were no legal problems entailed or any need for legal experts, whatever certain people seemed to think about it back in those times. My task was to ask for the transcript, to insist that the job was done in a timely fashion, and that was all I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your own recollection, when did you start your work as a secretary of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the secretary of the Municipal Assembly -- in order to answer your question, not only in respect of one ethnicity only, but in respect of all the ethnicities, that is, all of the deputies, all the people who participated in the work of the assembly. I started working on the 4th of January, 1991, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it be the 7th of January? May I please ask for exhibit Document S262. I wouldn't know myself when was assigned in 1992, but it was on or about -- the beginning of January 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned that you, no doubt, worked for the entire Municipal Assembly. Were you assigned to one or more individual persons?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have contacts with individuals on an individual basis, but I did have contacts with deputies generally speaking regardless of their function or office. As for the -- and in respect of the technical aspects of the work, those matters that were related to the work of the Municipal Assembly sessions. Other than that, I did not socialise with the deputies. I didn't go out for a drink or a coffee with them. I didn't have any personal or private contacts with the deputies either. I led an ordinary family life, just as I had prior to that period of time. That is, I socialised with my old friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could give us a little bit more insight of your work, I myself worked for a period of time also as a lawyer in the framework of a parliament. And I know what it is to exercise this more or less technical work in this area. Did you participate in meetings in the general -- in the assembly of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means. During the Municipal Assembly sessions, I would often -- I would normally sit next to the president and the deputy president of the Municipal Assembly in accordance with the usual procedure. It was a formal thing. And if necessary, if an explanation was needed, the seating arrangement was such that I was in a position to do it rapidly, to do it at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you have any assistance, and you were subordinate to whom, please?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not subordinate to anyone. I was the person in charge, the person who had been appointed by the assembly. I was responsible to the assembly as a whole. And it was my responsibility to fulfill and to carry out the technical aspect of the work that was necessary to be done for the municipality. As for the drafting of the decisions, no, I was not duty-bound to attend any such meetings because that fell within the scope of the responsibilities of the municipal organs who were each in charge of their department. So they were in charge of preparing their relevant decisions. They would send the drafts of those decisions to the executive committee, and the executive committee is an executive body of the Municipal Assembly which was composed of various professionals and representatives of various departments of the municipality who would then discuss the relevant proposals. If they decided that the matter should be discussed at the assembly, then a relevant proposal in terms of agenda would be presented and prepared for the assembly session. I did not have the authority to influence in any way the work of this executive body because it was the task of the leading person of the municipal organ of this administration to explain the reasons for any particular decision, why such decisions should be adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, did you have any personal assistants in order to help you with this entire work you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, when it was necessary to carry out the technical preparations for the assembly session which was a difficult work to do, the people from the technical services of the Municipal Assembly would prepare the working material; that is, they would take the material which had been prepared by the people from the executive body. And then they would prepare the draft agenda. But their work was mostly technical. They were in charge of copying the relevant material and distributing it to the deputies. They would put the documents in envelopes, and then send those materials to the deputies. They would also attend the assembly session. And after the session, they would carry out the work that had to be done upon the conclusion of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Municipal Assembly the first working day, who welcomed you in the Municipal Assembly? Can you recall it?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that any welcome was expressed to me by the president of the Municipal Assembly or the president of the executive council. I was simply informed that I had been appointed to the position of the secretary, although I had had no prior discussions with anyone as to whether I would accept the job or not. The reason I accepted the job was because I was unemployed at the time. It was a reasonable solution for me at the time. I went to the office which was earmarked for the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, and I had the relevant decision on my appointment. And I also received the salary for the secretary of the Municipal Assembly. It may sound a bit strange, but that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't believe it sounds strange. It sounds just normal, and one can understand that you felt pity as a lawyer to have to work as a secretary. But you mentioned just your office. Could the usher please be so kind and show the witness Exhibit S2 and S3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can offer to the Court if you find it helpful, we have a much larger blowup, but it is labelled, of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think for the reasons given earlier, yes, if you can show once again the two photos. Can you identify these two buildings?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is the building housing the Municipal Assembly, the one on the lower portion of the screen. And I can also see the entrance to the building. The one above also resembles this building, but the main entrance is somewhat less visible. But this is the building of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On my screen, I hardly can see the pictures. If you could have a look on the stills on the ELMO, please, and try once again to recognise what these buildings are on this apparatus at your left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the building in question, the one that I'm indicating just now. The building that I am now showing is the building housing the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the upper building, on the top of this page, the other still? Is this the same building from the other side, or...? Could you please assist us. Unfortunately, we are not able to ever be in Prijedor, and therefore it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't look like the building in question. I mean, it does, but I cannot see the entrance. There are trees in front of it which somehow don't -- I don't know. Maybe it's on the other side. It is possible that this is also the building in question, but I am not sure because I can see a street with trees. But the park which is outside the building, that is in front of the entrance of the building, is not very visible. It looks like the same building but the photograph must have been taken from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. We have to come back to this later. Thank you. Can you please tell us your office, was it on the ground floor or first floor? Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My office was located on the first floor on the northern side of the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was the president of the Municipal Assembly at the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And his deputy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And can you tell us now on the basis of that what happened in 1991 the development. You attended a meeting. There were some conclusions. How was this preceded? You already mentioned in part the work. When there was a decision made by the Municipal Assembly, who was in charge? Who was responsible, first, for the transcript, and then later for the formal presentation of the document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already explained the formal procedure. The minutes had to be processed, the minutes of the sessions had to be put in a written form and distributed. Also, the decision or a decision or a conclusion, depending on what was on the agenda, had to be made in accordance with the minutes. This was all signed by the president of the Municipal Assembly. That was his duty. The typing of the minutes and the typing of the decisions in the form they were adopted by the assembly in the original form was also done by typists. Once this document was signed, seals were placed on it, on the minutes and on the decisions themselves. And these documents were later sent to the relevant addressees, that is, to the individuals or bodies who were in charge of implementing those decisions.
