Let me give you an example: If, for example, the decision in question was the responsibility of the tax department, then it was the tax administration who initially -- who would initially draft and propose this decision. Then the decision was discussed by the executive body, and then if the discussions were positive, they would be sent to the assembly. When the assembly adopts the decision, then it becomes officially adopted by the assembly. Then it was typed, signed, and sealed, and sent back to the tax administration so that they can act upon it. If the decision, for example, involved the modalities of tax collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the documents were signed by the president. In case of the absence of the president, who was in charge? Who had to signed the documents then?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, this matter was stipulated in the statute of the municipality; but partly also in the rules of procedure. But mostly, it was regulated by the statute of the municipality. If it was a prolonged absence, then the deputy president of the assembly would become in charge of this, in the absence of the president. However, this did not happen in 1991 as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I recall very well about 20 years ago or so to a certain extent a similar position, and it was sometimes very difficult for me to find the person responsible for the signature. And was it also for you to find this person in order to get finally the necessary signature?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually we didn't have problems because regardless of the fact that the relevant decision did not reach its destination, the administrative clerks, that is, the clerks in charge of the department that had prepared the relevant material, would already start acting on it. So they could always wait 10 or 15 days for this decision to be officially signed. But they knew in advance what it was all about, and if necessary, prior to sending out the relevant ensuing documents, they would wait for the decision to be formally signed. So it was not always necessary to look for the signatory of the decision right away. We didn't have to get him as soon as possible all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that there were, as I understand it, several copies of these decisions, correct? To be sent out to the deputies?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you misunderstood me. I gave you the example of a tax matters' decision which concerned practically speaking only the relevant department, that is, the tax administration. Then there would be only one example of the decision which would be part of the working material and would be copied -- the necessary number of this decision would be copied, and the number corresponded to the number of the deputies. And once the work of the session was completed, that is, immediately after the end of the session, only two or three copies would be made because some copies would be sent to the files. And one copy would be sent to the body in charge. They could, then, make additional number of copies for their use. But apart from that, everything that was debated and decided upon at the assembly was also published in the official paper. So all of the interested parties had always -- always had the opportunity to get a copy of the relevant document and also to be informed of the matter. That is, the public, the citizens in general, had the right to be informed through the official paper, the Official Gazette, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just in case the president wouldn't have been there, and the document would have to be signed by a deputy or somebody else, or the special procedure, would this deputy sign with his own name or on behalf of the president?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can tell you about that because I don't remember. I did not have any such direct contacts. I mean, I was not in charge of taking such documents to the signatory. Those were usually done by various clerks. According to the statute, the president could do such a thing -- the deputy president could do such a thing if he wanted. But what happened really later, I don't know. I don't think it fell within the scope of my duties, and I don't think it was important for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You emphasised earlier that this never happened in 1991. Did it happen in 1992, or why did you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. So was there another development in 1992? I want to restrict this question now to the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, concerning our work, the procedure remained similar. Only if you're referring to the period, whatever it was called, the crisis period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You would fix which date with that what you call "the crisis period"? Would it be correct that there was a kind of change, on or about the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the assembly is concerned, it continued to function as an executive organ. Administration bodies also continued to operate. The procedure of drafting and adopting --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's crucial for this testimony because the translation shows that the Municipal Assembly continued to work -- to function as an executive organ. It's not what the witness said. So if you can try to clarify this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was: Would it be correct that there was a kind of change, on or about the 30th of April? And it reads on the transcript: "As far as the assembly is concerned, it continued to function as an executive organ." Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the 1st of January, 1992, throughout January, the assembly continued to operate just like it had operated in the period preceding that. Perhaps it was in April. I can't remember clearly. Sometime in April and May. I can't tell you the date exactly, but at some point, the Crisis Staff took over the role of the assembly. That's what the name of the body was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we come to the Crisis Staff, was there a change in the presidency in the Municipal Assembly as such?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a change in the sense that the president of the assembly as is clear from the decisions and the Official Gazette, this is -- should be easy to check who the president or the vice-president were at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you be so kind and tell us, to the best of your own recollection, and give us the names.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stakic was the president of the assembly, Milomir Stakic. And his deputy, vice-president, Dragan Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then I don't -- because I don't know what happened at that time, I therefore want to ask you once again to tell us in context what happened then on or about the 30th of April 1992, and the development then. You mentioned the word "Crisis Staff." Can you then tell us in context what happened, were there new organs? Was there a new division or distribution of labour? Were there additional organs in Prijedor? And please, tell us the entire development, your own experience until the end of your work in the Municipal Assembly, in context, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime between April and May, the change of the president of the assembly and the president of the municipality took place. How should I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. call it? Perhaps I can't find a fitting description now. At any rate, Mr. Stakic took over the position of Mr. Cehajic. What preceded this, because it is a generally known fact that there had been problems concerning the collaboration for the sake of everyone, I'm referring to those who had elected the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, could you continue. You mentioned now the change in the presidency. Was there an ongoing work of the assembly, work -- working as usual, we'll say, that you said seated, as you mentioned beforehand, beside the president in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly itself continued to exist, but its members were different. That means that this assembly was no longer composed of deputies of the SDA and the HDZ, as far as I can remember. The assembly continued to operate in the same or similar way as before until the Crisis Staff took over the functions of the assembly. The Crisis Staff, as we used to call it, a "mini assembly" that was put together according to a decision by the Crisis Staff. Until the beginning of 1991, this was referred to in the statute as "war presidency."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm again, sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the transcript it reads "1991." I think -- may it be correct that you want to say 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, but I have to make another objection concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because it says that there were -- that "the Crisis Staff is" -- I'm sorry. It says that it was a mini assembly that was put together according to a decision by the Crisis Staff. It's line 11, 12, 13. But the witness didn't say "the decision by the Crisis Staff." One body cannot compose itself. So if you can clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I think time for clarification is when it's for you to put questions to the witness. Until then, we have to rely --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's a translation problem; it's not a problem with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we ask the booth, was there anything misunderstood, or possibly misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have problems understanding this witness sometimes, so we are really not sure. This is what we heard, but it may not be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We just heard that it's difficult for our interpreters sometimes to follow you. Maybe it's better to come closer to the microphone. You said earlier when you discussed -- may I ask the same question once again. It was on the development 1991, 1992, the development from the Municipal Assembly to Crisis Staff, and then you mentioned the word "mini assembly." Could you please once again in the context tell us this development.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statute of the assembly, and I'm also referring to the statute that was used in 1991 and continued to be used and applied, this statute contained a chapter which said that in cases where extraordinary circumstances arose, so the assembly could not meet regularly, the role of the assembly would be assumed by the war presidency. This provision was amended. There was an amendment to the statute concerning that particular part of the statute. There was a decision by the assembly which said that that was the Crisis Staff. The composition of the Crisis Staff was envisaged, regulated, by this decision on amendments to the statute as well as the competencies of the Crisis Staff. Within the scope of its competencies were the same things that had been dealt with in the period preceding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before going into any further details, especially of your own work, could you please go on telling what happened after this, yes, transferral of the competencies to the Crisis Staff. What happened then? What was important for you and from your perspective in the Municipal Assembly? Please tell us in context, until you finalised your work with this Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, I think it was the month of May, that's the date that the decision bears, the decision on amendments to the statute, the function of the assembly was taken over by the Crisis Staff. And it performed this function on the premises of the Municipal Assembly, the administration. That way it was possible to perform this function with less people, and those were representatives of administration bodies. The Crisis Staff decided on proposals of administration bodies for decisions, conclusions, and solutions to be made. Perhaps the difference lay in the fact that draft decisions, proposals for decisions, were not drawn up in the form of work material, working material, and forwarded to the members of the staff. At least at the beginning, that's how it was. Rather, officials and decision-making officials of the municipal bodies provided verbal, oral, explanations at the -- during the sessions of the staff which was recorded. There was a record made of that, and the minutes were taken by hand. It was not -- the sessions were not tape recorded, and no shorthand version of the meetings were made. Of course, copies were made of this record, as I've said had been done also before. First it was typewritten, and then it was copied, and then it was further processed in the sense that these decisions were processed individually. And that was then distributed through the same channels as before. First, delivery to the relevant organs; then the stamping; and then the signing. All these jobs were within the competence of the administration bodies. I'll give you an example. The administration body in charge of education and health, we're talking about primary and secondary schools, when the director of this body was appointed, proposals would be given by the officials of that particular body. The Crisis Staff would discuss the proposal and proclaim its position concerning the appointment of the director. And then a decision was drafted concerning the appointment of director. This decision would then be forwarded to the school in question which had its own secretary, its own services, who would then forward this decision to all the relevant places where the decision needed to be forwarded. The same applied to the tax bodies, urban planning, traffic, and so on -- transport, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned the word "Crisis Staff" several times. Were you aware of the notion of "crisis committee" as well?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But once again, let's try to go through your work and how it continued. We are still with April, May 1992. Can you please tell us how long did you work for -- on behalf or for the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until February 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what happened in the meantime, say, from April, May 1992 until February 1993? Can you please, once again in context, try to give us some insight on the development in the Municipal Assembly at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The amendment to the statute that I have referred to, the part of it that refers to the Crisis Staff, among other things contained a list of persons who were members of the Crisis Staff. In my capacity as secretary of the assembly, I was not a member of this Crisis Staff. The technical aspect of the job of the Crisis Staff was performed by qualified people who were the technical service of the assembly. Why? Because, as I've already said, the role of the assembly was taken over by the Staff. I didn't even attend any sessions of the Crisis Staff except for a number of occasions when I was invited. That is -- I can't remember which sessions I did attend and which I did not. To the best of my recollection, I think it was in June, there was a session of the regular assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, again on the translation. The witness didn't say "June" but "July".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, did you want to say June or July? On the transcript --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: July, July. Yes, as far as I can remember, it was July. The regular assembly, perhaps it could have been convened at an earlier stage, but the need arose, so it was convened in July. Aside from the other issues discussed, it also verified the jobs, the tasks, that had been performed by the Crisis Staff during its operation. What I want to say is that the assembly confirmed the decisions, conclusions, adopted by the Crisis Staff. That is what I refer to as the "mini assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But when there was a session of the big assembly opposed to the as you call it mini assembly, you once again attended this assembly meeting in order to assist the president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that session, I can't remember attending that session. But I suppose so. Perhaps I have forgotten. Yes, I suppose I was to attend that meeting in my capacity as secretary of the assembly. But I'm not sure whether I did attend or not. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to these details later. Just to follow up, what happened then later? Were there regular meetings of the Municipal Assembly, following July?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly continued to operate according to need during the period of my presence there. In 1993, I left the assembly and returned to my previous employer. I think it was late March -- early March or late February, I'm talking about the last session I attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there, once again, another change in the presidency during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a change. The change took place exactly when I left the assembly. I think that's when the change took place, the change of the secretary. I do not know whether at that session in early March or late February, whether that's when the new president was appointed or any other appointments or perhaps, should I say vice-president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of the new president and vice-president.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Dusan Kurnoga was the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what were the reasons for this change, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons were probably internal reasons within the assembly, reasons among the deputies. Those must have been the reasons that led to changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So that there is no misunderstanding, it was a change in the presidency from Dr. Stakic to Dusan Kurnoga. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, that's correct. And Radanovic became the vice-president. His nickname was Cigo. I can't remember his first name now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to make a break now. For your better understanding, it's necessary to have this break in order to facilitate especially the life of our interpreters, and we'll have a break until 2.30. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. Mr. Baltic, before the break, we learned that you left the same time when Dr. Karadzic was substituted by another president, and we had also another vice-president. You quoted the names. Can you give us the reasons for this change, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry. It might confuse the witness. You said Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you for this. Dr. Stakic, of course.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My departure and the time when I left the assembly has nothing to do with Mr. Stakic or Mr. Karadzic, as you said. Just an aside. The reason of my departure was purely private and personal nature. At the beginning, I believe I emphasised the fact that the work of a secretary of this kind did not really suit me as a lawyer by profession because I couldn't prove myself as a lawyer by doing this type of work. I'm not saying that it was humiliating, nothing of that sort; it was just a temporary solution for me. In view of the fact that there were problems in the work of the deputies, it was very difficult to listen to them and to follow and monitor their work. I had already thought of trying to find another job; however, circumstances being as they were, this was very difficult. These conflicts lasted for a while, for at least several months. I'm -- it's not really conflicts -- there were disagreements, differences amongst the deputies. But most of these differences were of a personal nature. Let me tell you what I'm referring to. Certain people had influential positions, held influential offices, and through the performance of their work, they were able to exert certain amount of influence over the way the resources were spent, in particular I'm referring to the humanitarian aid which was not a negligible issue, after all. There were attempts on the part of certain people to obstruct the work, generally speaking. And that is the reason why certain individuals wanted the top official to be replaced by a different set of individuals. Again, it was all the issue of personal interests. On one, two, or perhaps more occasions, it proved -- it turned out that it was no longer possible for the assembly to continue functioning normally. And that was the reason why I wanted to abandon my position there. I no longer wanted to listen to their useless discussions. This happened at the time when certain individuals decided to abandon their positions. I personally wanted to get rid of that because it was a very thankless position in terms of cooperation with both factions. To my regret, I was returned to my original employer which at the time was just another bankrupt company. Others were given opportunity to find something better. I did not wish to beg anyone for anything and I returned, as I said, to my original company where I used to work. So that would more or less constitute the reason for my departure, my personal dissatisfaction, lack of understanding amongst the deputies, and the employees of the assembly generally speaking and so on and so forth. My departure, once again, had nothing to do with the fact that one set of individuals were leaving and others were coming to take their places. And this new set did not carry on in the same manner. I believe that this is enough as an explanation as to how my departure coincided with the departure of certain deputies and officials. People thought that I was sitting on the fence, but I was really neither here nor there. And I found myself left to my devices. I had to fend for myself as best I could. I believe that this has provided you with a sufficient explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You just mentioned "individuals were leaving." To be concrete and to give these individuals names, can you tell us something about the reasons why Dr. Stakic left? Did he leave voluntarily, or was he dismissed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that the conflict, that is, a misunderstanding, that occurred between Mr. Stakic and an elderly gentleman there, an elderly deputy, senior deputy, to the assembly, Srdjo Garaca [phoen]. Srdjo Garaca [phoen] insisted that Stakic should no longer be the president for the materialistic reasons. There were no other reasons whatsoever. It all had to do with the way the resources, including the humanitarian aid, were distributed and allocated. The situation lasted for a while. I cannot tell you exactly how long, but I'm sure it was long enough. The work of the assembly was blocked. The assembly was in a deadlock. I remember that there was a break for lunch, like the one we had here today, and following this lunch break, Mr. Stakic resigned. As I said, the reasons were purely personal. I'm sure that there were probably people who thought -- who believed that after this change had taken place, they would be able to exert more influence over the course of the events to serve their interests. I was sickened by all this. And I realised that I should no longer be part of that, part of all this nonsense. And that was enough for me to say goodbye to the assembly. As to who other individuals were, well, it soon turned out who they were. There was Momcilo Radanovic, deputy president of the assembly, and others. But I really tried not to think about it for a while, and after all, it was ten years ago, and I managed to forget a certain number of things including probably the important ones. As I said, it was Cigo Radanovic who became the deputy president after the change, and Dusan Kurnoga became the president after Mr. Stakic. Of course this entailed obviously the president of the executive and the deputy president of the executive board. So this is how it happened. I left, and moreover, I stopped following the work of the assembly in general because it was no longer of any use to me. It only -- it could have only caused me additional headaches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Easy to understand. Can we please try once again to clarify some notions we addressed this morning already. Please correct me if I misunderstood you. First, there was a Municipal Assembly. Then we had a Crisis Staff. Then you told us about a meeting of the Municipal Assembly confirming or endorsing some decisions of the Crisis Staff. Were there held any more meetings of the Crisis Staff after this meeting, once again, of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, you want to know whether after the process of confirmation of all of the decisions adopted by the Crisis Staff during the period of time when the Crisis Staff was in charge of adopting such decisions, whether after that period of time the Crisis Staff continued with its work. Well, it could no longer operate. It was no longer legal because according to the statute, in times when Municipal Assembly was not able to convene, then the Crisis Staff would become operational. However, once the conditions are met for the assembly to convene and work, then the Crisis Staff no longer functioned. So that's how the Municipal Assembly convened on -- I don't remember the exact date, but it was in the month of July. And it was presented with the work of the Crisis Staff. Everything was there on paper, all of the decisions and the conclusions that had been adopted by the Crisis Staff. All these were analysed and discussed by the Municipal Assembly and eventually confirmed -- rather, adopted by the assembly as something legal and legitimate. So I believe this is clear. After this session of the assembly, it was no longer -- I mean, it was not possible for two organs of this kind to function simultaneously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then just once again, for clarification, what was the function and when did it actually act of the so-called war presidency?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that this is the third time that I'm trying to make myself clear. The war presidency or the Crisis Staff we can call it, it's one and the same body with two different titles, so that body performed the work which would have normally been performed by the Municipal Assembly. The Municipal Assembly was left with the work of various administrative bodies, various departments. They also dealt with various private initiatives, proposals given by the citizens and so on and so forth. Let me give you an example. There was a problem with the distribution of fuel at the time. Because in those days, it was possible for certain individuals to come to the petrol station and take as much fuel as they wanted without paying for it. And of course, this irritated the population, so there was a private proposal, private initiative of that kind, which was presented to the assembly. And it was decided that the distribution of petrol -- of oil and oil products could not be done everywhere. And this was the responsibility of the organ in charge of economy and finances. So this was dealt with by that particular department. And the person in charge of this department was authorised to give specific permissions as to the quantity of fuel that could be issued to such and such individuals or companies. So those were the very specific problems that were dealt with very specific departments of the Municipal Assembly. This was just one example which I believe illustrates sufficiently enough the kind of work that was performed by other organs. They didn't do anything that would have fallen outside the scope of their normal duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You will understand that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, objection to the translation. Page 66 line 2 and line 10, I don't know why, but the witness said "Crisis Staff" and it's translated "Municipal Assembly". The first time "assembly" and the second time "Municipal Assembly". Could you clarify this with the witness please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could give me the line please, once again. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 66, line 2, and line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to ask you about -- you mentioned that "this irritated the population, so there was a private proposal, private initiative, of that kind which was presented to the assembly". Is it correct that it was presented to the assembly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may explain, this was general knowledge. I mean, we all knew that these things happened. And if something was so publicly known, then of course the issue became known to the department in charge. So it was perfectly normal for the person who was in charge of that specific department, for instance, in this case, the person in charge of economy and finances, to become aware of that. So a solution needed to be found. I don't know whether he personally or in cooperation with his associates was in a position to propose, to make an adequate proposal to the executive body which then forwarded the issue to the Crisis Staff. The issue -- the idea, of course, in this case was to put a stop to this practice which eventually resulted in an adequate decision that this distribution of oil products could only take place at one particular location. A relevant document was also produced which was signed by the person in charge of these affairs. So eventually there was only one distribution point for oil and oil products in the area. The idea was to avoid having various kinds of individuals going to the petrol station and obtaining fuel for their personal needs. I believe that was the idea behind this practice. I believe this is clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before coming to the second question by the Defence counsel as regards interpretation, you will understand that I'm eager to know who were these certain individuals who had the possibility to come to petrol stations and "take as much fuel as they wanted to without paying for it."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who were they? It's difficult for me at this point to remember who these specific individuals were. But for instance if someone was driving someone, a municipal official or someone else in charge, they would go to the petrol station, and then they said: "Well, I need fuel for this person." And they would present him with a piece of paper, and then sign this paper. I mean, I would have never taken such responsibility of taking fuel without appropriate papers. So a regulations had to be passed, a regulation had to be adopted to avoid this type of behaviour in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did this possibility of a very special kind of self-service exist already before the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were very difficult times. They were difficult because the economy was already functioning under very difficult circumstances. Expenses had to be cut down in view of the general circumstances. The whole economy had to be rationalised, and this was the idea behind this decision as well. After that, things functioned normally more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: My question was, was there a change before the, as we call it here in the courtroom unanimously "the takeover" and after the takeover as regards -- you gave on your own initiative these examples, and therefore I wanted to come back to this example. Was this a new problem, this self-service, after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, it was not my initiative. It was a generally known fact that we were short of all sorts of supplies, not merely oil and oil products. It was in all the different areas that serious work needed to be done to stop this trend. And even earlier, there were such cases where fuel was allocated according to the purposes it was to be used for. I remember the case of agriculture. It was said that priority needed to be given as far as the use of fuel was concerned to those dealing with agriculture, and there had to be some sort of monitoring and control. And that in certain other areas where it turned out that more fuel was being used up than seemed necessary, it was said that vehicles should be used less. And what it boiled down to eventually was that those who wanted could be allocated a certain amount of petrol. And if I space this out, my use of fuel over a certain period, after that I was no longer able to obtain any more petrol. They would just put a lock on my car and I had to move about in whichever way I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, and please answer with yes or no: Was this problem of self-service by certain individuals, as you called it, a problem, a special or specific problem, for the period of time after the 30th of April? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem was present before also. But it wasn't stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's leave it at this point in time with this answer. We may come back to this on the basis of maybe a document. So we were on our avenue to clarify some notions. And I think we succeeded to a certain extent. Was the Prijedor Municipal Assembly at any point in time renamed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was always called the Municipal Assembly. Only the period that we referred to, it was the Crisis Staff that made decisions on behalf of the Municipal Assembly. And we explained what exactly this Crisis Staff was and how it worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever heard about a Serbian Republic of Krajina, Autonomous Region, Prijedor Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Municipal Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Prijedor as far as I know never existed. As far as the autonomous republic, I think that's what you said, of Krajina, yes, I did hear about that, but let me put it this way: I'm not sure it affected the work of the assembly in any way because I think the assembly always occupied itself with the jobs entailed in the current laws. And it was always trying to deal with the problems on hand of the -- that the administrative bodies had to deal with. It tried to stick to the laws that had been in place before. If there were any problems with taxes and with tax collection, what was the most interesting municipal organ for this was the organ dealing with the collection of taxes. There were problems at that point, and we were trying to improve, to find new ways to improve the functioning of this, of the collection of taxes, for the collection to be carried out. We were looking for a possibility to collect the taxes due by citizens, and some citizens were simply evading this. So it was requested to have a decision on how exactly to collect. There were a number of very drastic cases where this needed doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you. You may know, your time and also our time is limited, and I would kindly ask you to concentrate on the questions. And I just had asked you whether you ever heard about a Serbian Republic Krajina, autonomous region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry. I think it's the way Your Honour is putting it. It's actually the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. I am quoting from a document. I have a document, Serbian Republic Krajina, Autonomous Region, Prijedor Municipal Assembly. Maybe it's the wrong translation. To facilitate this, and to avoid any misunderstandings, may the usher please present Exhibit S262 on the ELMO. Can we please zoom to the top of the page. Higher, higher. That we can read -- yes. Now it's fine. If you could please have a look on the apparatus beside you, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Dated the 8th of September, 1992, upper left corner, it reads: "Serbian Republic, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, committee for appointments and nominations. Number 01-11-333/92. Date: The 8th of September, 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen such or similar documents?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've had no opportunity to see exactly this sort of document, but I can't say that the concept of the Autonomous Region of Krajina is unfamiliar to me. In my opinion, it was neither a republic nor could it pass regulations the way a republic could -- regulations that could be binding for anyone. And I don't know how they would have been binding for the municipal organs since the municipal organs were guided by material provisions from their own field, sphere of competence. So as a republic, it seems impossible that there would be enough time to deal with all the legal issues in all the different spheres of life and to provide guidance and regulations and to have these as prescriptions that -- provisions, legal provisions that would be above any other legal provisions. So I do not have any precise insight into the way it worked, but I cannot claim that I have never heard the name "Autonomous Region of Krajina" used, no. I don't know who the leader of this Autonomous Region of Krajina was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we move to the end of the text, please. What can we read there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, in the lower right corner, it reads: "President of the committee, Dragan Savanovic" personally. This was during the period of the assembly's work. He was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. How he got to sign this, I have no idea. In the upper left corner where it says "Prijedor" and then "subject: opinion concerning the appointment of officials," someone is requesting something. I really don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Help us, please, with this: Following the name on the bottom line, we find SR in Cyrillic with two dots. What does this mean, "SR"?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means "personally," in his own hand. This abbreviation is used when documents are published in the Official Gazette. So you don't publish their acts that had actually been signed but only those which had gone through the procedure and those that had gone down in the minutes. So only that is published in the Official Gazette. Where this came from, I really can't tell you because if it was in the Municipal Assembly, then it is clear that a decision like this must have, in the lower right corner, the president of the assembly and not the vice-president. And this is the president of the committee. So I think this doesn't even deserve to be published in the Official Gazette. This is just a document which I have no idea how it -- where it came from. Maybe it came from Dragan Savanovic directly. If he was in charge of education, if he had his tasks in that field, whether this is how he went about his business, I don't know how. Maybe he was convinced that this was the way to do it and he never -- it never occurred to him to consult anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. When we are just with this SR, may I kindly ask the usher to put on the ELMO another document -- no, I'll give it to you. Leave it on the ELMO, this document. Just one other document with the ERN number 0014153. It's included in the list of colour copies. And may this be, please, put on the ELMO so that we can see the signature. Could you please help us with this. Here, we don't see SR, but something different. Could you please -- I can't read it on my screen. What you can see and identify. Possibly also in this case it's more helpful to look on the document on the apparatus beside you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you blow this up for me, please. I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So please, turn around to the apparatus, and indicate there --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm only interested now in this SR or however it reads. "Za." What's the meaning of this as opposed to SR?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not really clearly legible. But in the first line, the first word I don't even know what it means, and underneath, it reads "Municipal Assembly." Whether the word above that is president, I have no idea. It's not very clear. And as for this, Milomir Stakic, well, okay, could be. This could indeed be his name and surname during his stint as a president. And then someone wrote "za" here which means that someone else signed on behalf of him. And now how someone could have signed in his name on behalf of him with no permission, no authorisation, perhaps if he wasn't there. So if there is a vice-president standing in for the president during prolonged absences, perhaps that can be the case. But if the president is just gone for a short while and this other person, the vice-president, seizes the opportunity saying "I'm the vice-president, I can go about this any way I like," and just sign the document and the lower-ranking official puts a stamp on it because he has to, he is made to, and then it's supposed to be a binding document. But this here, we should see -- study exactly how it was done, whether it was done during a prolonged absence of the president so he was nowhere to be found to sign this document. I really don't know. That's my opinion. And as far as the word "za," meaning for, that means for the president signed by the vice-president. Whether this is his signature or not, Savanovic's signature, I don't know. I can't see who signed this. What it says is: "Za, Dr. Milomir Stakic." For Dr. Milomir Stakic, and then a signature. I don't know. I couldn't really say. It seems rather illegible. You can't see it clearly. I don't know this person who signed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't want to go into details of this concrete signature. Just opposed to this za, that we are clear and in line with what we are discussing. May we now turn, please, to the previous document which was signed "SR." And then turn to page 2, if you could, please, read page 2. Please, also once again on the apparatus, it will be easier for you to read. It's not readable, I'm afraid. Can you see your own name?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kreca [phoen], I can't see my name here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you read the headline, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "List of officials nominated by the Municipal Assembly on the 16th of April, 1992, and nominated by other relevant authorities -- appointed by other relevant authorities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we now turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see my name under number 1, my first and last name, and this is related to, as you can see, the list of officials appointed by the Municipal Assembly. And then number 1, Dr. Milomir Stakic, Kovacevic, Savanovic, Baltic as the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, the 7th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then, at the end, what does it -- no, no. In the same line, one can read: "Baltic" and then secretary. Correct? And then --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Baltic, Dusan, secretary of the Municipal Assembly. Appointed on the 7th of January, 1992 for a period of up to four years." I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This should be a clarification opposed to the English translation we have available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know that his translation is better. Theirs is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, I think we should listen what the witness has to tell us. And I think this is a more reliable source, and if there is a translation problem, we have to come back to this, only that we know that there is a problem. Now, we can see 7 January, 1992. For a period up to four years, as you mentioned. Now, let's turn to page 1 of the same document once again. Can't we see here that this was a document dated 8 September, 1992? And how is it possible to have an appointment at this point in time for January 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I can't explain this, nor am I familiar with this, that after a certain period of time has elapsed, the date. I can see here, the 8th of September, 1992. It reads: "Serbian Republic," that is, Serbian Democratic Party, BH, municipal board of Prijedor, Prijedor. And again, this has nothing to do with me because I am not a member of the SDS. It's possible that this was the case, but how, I really couldn't explain. The 8th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, was there --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I only heard "this document." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your observation is quite correct. I can't explain to myself how in this period, in September 1992, there was a document like this to be signed here underneath. In the lower left corner, it says: "President of the committee." I am not familiar that there were any proposals concerning myself, nor did I attend any meeting, if we're talking about SDS meetings, because I never attended those and I was not a member. But I can say that I always worked as secretary, and I can't comment why there was a very vivid flow of different people in the positions of president and vice-president of the assembly. If someone else proposed me for any of those positions, that was without informing me. I was just a simple official the same as 250 other people who were going about their jobs. They were clerks. And no one let those positions because the president and -- the positions and president and vice-president were changed. There were 250 or 300 working in the municipal administration, we couldn't just say,"okay, we'll quit work today and" allow ourselves to be thrown out into the street and just go and look for a different job. People in those positions, in the positions of clerks, no one asks them anything. They were not influential. I could see this in my own case. I was just a simple clerk. I had several people who did this type of work with me, the work of a clerk. And how politics affected this, we really didn't go very deep in a that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify on the basis of this document whether or not either in September 1992 or in January 1992, there was some change as to the working conditions or the employer? Did you, to the best of your recollection, remember any such change, be it in September or January?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September, in my opinion, it would have been impossible that anything like that should have occurred. I have no information to that effect. As far as January is concerned, on the basis of my presence there, it was not a body of administration. Dragan Savanovic was supposed to sign this, but not as the vice-president of the assembly but as an SDS member which was completely unrelated to the work of the administrative organs. His position in the SDS would not have entitled him to work in any sense with administrative bodies. So it strikes me as strange I see my own name written here, but I was secretary between January 1991 and March 1993, and I have already given you my reasons why I accepted this position and why I left eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The purpose of this line of questions was indeed whether or not there was a change and whether, and please answer this last question on this issue, you got a new contract in 1992 substituting an earlier contract.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never got any contract. My employment as a secretary began in January 1991. And throughout that period of time, I was the secretary of the Municipal Assembly. As for the changes of the president and the vice-president, as you can see I recorded -- I never received any formal decision, any signed decision, to that effect. I don't know whether it exists. I would like to see it. Throughout those months, January, February, and up until the end of 1992, I performed the duties of the secretary, as I explained. I mean, I described the role of the secretary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... May we now turn once again to another issue. In the Municipal Assembly, was there any kind of dress code?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I always wore civilian -- a civilian suit. I didn't have any weapon, nor did I have any uniform. I was dressed the same way as I'm dressed today except that I had probably a different colour suit. I don't remember what colour it was. But it was a civilian suit. And this is how I dressed for work. I didn't live very far from my place of work, some three or four hundred metres away. Sometimes I would go by car, my personal car. But most of the time, I went to work on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier as to the fact that you were not a member of the Crisis Staff, you attended in general not these meetings. But here and then, you had access to these meetings. Did you see the persons present there in uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, no, I don't remember seeing anyone wearing a uniform. It may have happened at the times when certain individual officials did wear a uniform. But not in their official civilian capacity. They didn't wear uniform when they went to work. Whether they wore a uniform outside the municipality, that's their business. Or if they went to a different municipality, I don't know. I didn't have an opportunity to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try to be more concrete. Who were the members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it is in dispute. You probably have documents which specifically enumerate people who were by virtue of their function members of the Crisis Staff. I think that that was the president of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Municipal Assembly, the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, and all leaders or individuals in charge of specific departments. This regulation was in place even before the war, and I believe that such a regulation applies even today. It probably -- the body in question has a probably different name. It's no longer a Crisis Staff, but I think that those would have been the people who by virtue of their functions were members of the Crisis Staff. At least, this is how it was in 1991. At that time, the body was called the war presidency, and, well, we didn't like the name of the body because it sounded too socialist or communist, and that's why we changed the name. But we also got the idea from the neighbouring countries, from Croatia, for instance. Where the idea came from originally, I don't know. Why the body was eventually called the Crisis Staff, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But let's concentrate on those persons you call until now only individuals. There are, in this procedure, contested documents and noncontested documents. And therefore, it's to a certain extent important to know from you, to the best of your recollection, who in person were actually members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the third or the fourth time that I have to repeat myself. I don't know how come the matter is still unclear, that is, that the members of the war presidency or the Crisis Staff were people who occupied certain positions. The same rule applied during the period preceding 1990. But before that time, the regulation was never applied in practice, that is, that the function of the assembly was taken over in extraordinary circumstances, that is, if the deputies were unable to meet, if the assembly was unable to convene, then this regulation would be applied. That is, those who were able to convene would convene and would debate the same matters which would have normally been debated by the Municipal Assembly. So that group of people -- that staff would be then in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Call the Crisis Staff mini assembly. The only thing I wanted to hear from you are what are the names of this mini assembly, participants in this mini assembly you called the Crisis Staff, only the names without any additional comments.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should look at the decision on the establishment of the -- on the functioning of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the first sentence of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, I asked you to the best of your recollection, what are the names of the members of the Crisis Staff. We are not interested in contested or not contested documents. We are interested in what you experienced in 1992. And I'm quite sure you know the names of these persons.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, it was the people who had certain functions who were members of the Crisis Staff. Therefore, the president of the assembly, who at the time was Dr. Milomir Stakic; his deputy was Dragan Savanovic; the president of the executive board, Kovacevic; his deputy, Mr. Mandic; secretary for economic affairs, Mr. Travar. I don't know who were the members of other organs. And also the persons in charge of other departments. I don't know, for instance, who the person in charge of town planning and land survey was. I don't know who those people were at the time. I don't know who was the person in charge of the revenue administration. There were many changes going on at the time. So that's why I cannot remember who those people were. But it would have been also the person in charge of the defence, which was also a municipal body. That is, the body for national defence. That was that. And the police, of course, which is also one of the municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Judge Schomburg, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, because the interpreters didn't get my question because my microphone wasn't on, could you please add the names to the representative of the national defence and the police.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the police is concerned, I think that it was Mr. Drljaca. And as for the defence, it was Mr. Budimir. I'm not quite sure, but I think that those were the ones because there were very frequent changes in certain departments. So I'm not quite sure, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again the question is not whether you attended a meeting, but have you ever been in a room when there was a meeting of the Crisis Staff? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would from time to time find myself in a room of that kind, but I don't know what meetings those were. So I cannot remember at the moment what it was. But again, those people who were in charge of specific municipal organs, and we know exactly which organs these are, and it should not be difficult to find the relevant information, that is, to find out who was in charge of which specific municipal body. Because if I say that so and so was a member, I may be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... That during this period of time, it was not the case that, as it was earlier and how it was later, than when there was such a meeting, you sat beside the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. Can you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, I will. You mentioned earlier that in a regular meeting of the Municipal Assembly, in your function as secretary, you were seated beside the president. My question is now: When there is a meeting, when there was a meeting of a Crisis Staff, did it never happen that you were seated beside Dr. Stakic acting in his capacity as president of the Municipal Assembly and at the same time member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained on several occasions that while I was the secretary of the Municipal Assembly, while the assembly was still working, that it was my duty to attend the assembly as provided for in the statute. As for the decision on the Crisis Staff, I was not a member of the Crisis Staff, nor did I have the obligation to attend the meetings of the Crisis Staff. I didn't say that I didn't attend some of the meetings when certain issues were being debated and decided upon because after all, it was not my obligation to attend, nor was it important. But furthermore, now I cannot remember what meeting it was, the one that I attended, but I know that the sessions were recorded by the recording secretary who had to attend such meetings. And that record, those minutes, would be typed out. And after the minutes were typed out, then the individual decisions were dealt with. Because at the bottom of each such document, each of the minutes, you can see the name of the recording secretary. That is, who took the minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. You mentioned that you attended one meeting. Once again, the question: The people participating in this meeting, did one or more of them wear uniforms at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: At those meetings which I attended, those very rare meetings, I cannot remember anyone wearing a uniform. If someone was a member of the Crisis Staff, and that could be someone who, according to the statute and until 1990, that was always a representative of the military. That is, the person who was in charge of the military affairs on behalf of the municipality, the person who is in charge, for instance, of keeping adequate records concerning the military affairs. The records of future conscripts, for instance. That was always the case, as it is still today. As to whether anyone ever wore a uniform at a meeting, it is possible, but at this point, I really don't know, I cannot answer your question. I don't remember seeing anyone. I mean, if the individual in question was the representative of the military or the barracks, that is, then he would probably wear a uniform if this was indeed his official uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly this morning that your office was located at the first floor of the building? It was the same floor --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- Where Dr. Stakic had his office. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the same floor, but on the other side, maybe 10 metres away in the opposite direction, that is, on the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In your function as secretary, had you often to go to the office of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, except when I was invited. As I have already said, it was never my custom to have coffee with anyone, neither during the work nor after the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it can facilitate if --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- If you answer more directly. So on the basis of your answer, you said: "Except when I was invited." Had you been invited once or several times to his office?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in 1991, up until February 1992, I was sometimes invited --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's please concentrate on the --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was not invited because there was no need for us to discuss the meetings in any way. I already explained to you that the session of the Crisis Staff was convened in such a way that the president or his deputy or their secretary, the lady secretary who was also working on the switchboard, and I presume it was -- in most of the cases her who issued the invitations for the people to attend the meeting because she was working with the telephone. So those people would meet and then decide on the issues that were on the agenda. There were no legally unclear situations that any further clarifications were needed. As I said, it was all very technical. There were no written proposals of decisions who would be forwarded to the interested parties by the technical service. But it was in this other manner, I mean, I assume that it was the secretary who called people by the phone, then they would attend the meeting. They would expose the issue orally, and relevant notes or minutes were also taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I think we should really concentrate, and I think you understand my questions, on the question and give us a short and precise answer. My next question would be who occupied or sat in the office opposed to the office of Dr. Stakic on the same corridor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offices of the president and the vice-president were on the same side, on the south side of the building. Between these two offices, there was the room occupied by the secretary, that is, the person who communicated by telephone with both of them, and also with external users, that is, citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen the president or the vice-president in these premises with uniform, wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I never entered these premises if I was not invited. And neither officially nor privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see one of these persons in the building, the municipal -- in the building of the Municipal Assembly in uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I indicated a moment ago that one of the members of the Crisis Staff was also the representative of the local barracks. I don't know exactly what his name was, but that was his regular uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I asked you quite clearly with respect to Dr. Stakic and the vice-president. Did you ever see these two persons in uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In their office, I cannot remember having seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I asked you, in the building.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building. In the building. I cannot remember having seen them in uniform because there was no need for anyone to don a uniform if they were involved in their civilian work. Whether something of the kind happened in the afternoon or when I was not there or if people went outside the building, that is possible. But as I said, during that period of time, during that crisis period, I did my best to see that the work is done appropriately. I spent most of the time in my office, and after that I would go home because I did not have a habit of frequenting cafes. I led a normal family life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably you can rethink during the next break your answer. And I have to remind you that you are under solemn declaration. But before we have the break, let me finally turn to the notions where I started the line of questions. May I ask the usher to bring the following document with the ERN number 00633803 on the ELMO, please. This is 65 ter number 271. Could you please be so kind and read out this document, because it's extremely difficult for us with our limited knowledge --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Prijedor Municipality. Technical services of the Municipal Assembly. 30th of June, 1992, Simo Drljaca, public security station. "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality has tasked these services to draft the information on the implementation of these conclusions, orders, decisions, and conclusions, reached and passed at its sessions. In order for the technical services to draft this information, it requested on writing on the 23rd of June, 1992, data concerning the implementation of the said conclusions of the Crisis Staff of which you are responsible and which were forwarded to you in a timely manner. "As, however, you have to this day not delivered the information required, you should do it by the 1st of July, 1992, so that the services could carry out their duty. "Secretary of the Municipal Assembly," then my first and last name. If I can just keep this here for a moment longer, I would like to see the upper part of the document again because there's a stamp here. And it reads: "Secretary of the Municipal Assembly, Dusan Baltic." If I can, please, just have the upper part again. Technical services. You can raise it a little bit so I can see the text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading the text again.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Requested by who? The services, I don't know. On the 23rd of June, 1992, to forward this information in writing, so I don't understand this conclusion here with my name, my first and last name underneath. But yes, I could say that in July, if this is about the drafting of all conclusions, what the assembly, that is, the Crisis Staff, as I have said before, did, that was verified in July which means verification. That in that document, there should be a survey of all conclusions, decisions passed by the Crisis Staff, and then that is forwarded to the assembly so the assembly can review that. And then the assembly should either say: "We confirm this" or "we don't." But the technical services never monitored the implementations of these decisions, absolutely never. If there was something decided and regulated by a decision, technical services never monitored the implementation of any such decisions. This could only be monitored by those who it applied to. Whether this was a municipal organ, when a decision applied to a municipal organ as we have stated before, because proposals of conclusions and decisions were passed by municipal bodies. And when those were passed, those organs would receive these decisions and they worked on their implementation. So they were the only bodies who were in a position to provide an explanation concerning the implementation or nonimplementation. So every municipal organ was supposed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Baltic. We will come to this decision, indeed, we are aware of this, later. Showing you this document, I only wanted to ask you whether you would agree that from this document, we can infer that you yourself acted under the headline "Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Prijedor Municipality, Municipal Assembly professional" -- or as you said "technical services". Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I must repeat. As we're talking about the 30th of June, 1992, at that time, the assembly -- regular, now I can't say now whether they had a session or not. But as far as I can remember they could meet regularly and work regularly. And this is demonstrated by the document on the verification and confirmation of all decisions taken by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to turn on the microphone, at the very least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to have the break now. And we will have time enough to come to this document later. My only really very last question is do you contest the authenticity of this document you have before you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do pose this question, because I don't understand what the purpose is and who is requesting what from whom? On the basis of this, it would seem that the technical services were requiring from -- I have no idea. I don't understand this text or the date, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are not interested in the text. We are interested in the question: Did you sign this document? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember this document. All I can see is my name typed there, secretary of the assembly, Dusan Baltic. And then the signature which looks very much like mine. But truth to tell, this seems very dubious to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It will probably assist you in thinking back to some of your answers whether you have to make a correction or not. We have a break now until 20 minutes to 5.00, and then proceed until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. In our schedule, we have today's hearing until 4.00, and I have some commitments with the newly established bar association at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is true, I'm afraid, for all of us that we have some commitments. But priority has to be given that all the parties have the possibilities to put questions to the witness before us. And I hope that I can conclude the line of questions today, and only this allows us to hopefully to conclude tomorrow. As you all know on Friday, there is no possibility, because no courtroom is available. And therefore, all participants were kind enough, as I just learned, that we can proceed until 5.30. And as to the enormous amount of costs connected with this procedure, we have to proceed this way. The deposition taking stays adjourned until 4.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Baltic, let us now please turn to a more technical question. You already indicated what was your duty as secretary. But now we want to turn to the question, documents of the Prijedor Municipality. No doubt, they were published. Can you tell us a little bit about the procedure of publishing documents and who was responsible for sending documents to or for the purpose of publication to either the Official Gazette or, as one can see sometimes, Kozarski Vjesnik or Glas? Who was responsible for sending out the documents for publication?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distribution of documents, regardless of whether these documents were adopted by the assembly or the Crisis Staff, was the responsibility of the technical services; that's, the employees of the technical services. This entailed having copies made of the minutes, transcribing the minutes, and then drafting individual documents. This was done by employees, typists, simple clerks and legal officers. Legal officers were in charge of -- when copying from the minutes to the decision, to check whether everything matched. As far as the stamping and the signing of the documents was concerned, then usually simple clerks were used to deliver these documents for stamping and signing. As far as the publishing of these documents is concerned, during the period of the operation of the assembly, as I've said before, every document that was adopted was published in the Official Gazette formally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let us now turn to this very technical issue. May the usher present on the ELMO Exhibit Number S69, just one example. May we please see it in a way that we can see the entire document. And please, Mr. Baltic, would you please be so kind, and once again, we are not interested in the content of this document, but turn to the top of the page, what we can read at the top of the page on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and read it.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reference is made on one of the orders in the upper left corner you have Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Autonomous Region of Krajina, Prijedor Municipality, number and date, the 6th of June, 1992, pursuant to article 7 on the decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then at the bottom, the signature.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Past the order, signature, president of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you recognise the signature of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with his signature, but it may as well be his. There is a number of documents that were signed before, so I don't think that's a problem. In the upper left corner, you see that pursuant to Article 7 of the decision on the Crisis Staff, with all its areas of competence listed it, it reads that on the basis of Article 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't want to address the content. Just go once again to the signature. A minute before, you mentioned that there is a number of documents that were signed before. What do you want to express by saying this?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY [Resumed]
